Its designer, Roland Lamb, was inspired by waves, which are at once continuous and marked by discrete peaks and troughs, and he wanted a digital keyboard that could play individual notes and also explore the space between them. He put forward the idea of a 'living instrument', holding that an instrument only means something if a community of players keeps using it, and that otherwise it is like a dead object in a museum. His thinking also refers to the early critics who, when the piano appeared at the end of the eighteenth century, thought it too hard to play; he wanted to offer accessible depth of expression so that users learn as they play. Later products grew into small twenty-four-key models, twenty-five- and forty-nine-key models and an eighty-eight-key model, and gained such changes as Bluetooth wireless MIDI, a built-in rechargeable battery and, on some models, a built-in sound engine.

The Seaboard is a keyboard-style MIDI controller and synthesiser made by the British company ROLI, an electrophone among electronic keyboards. It replaces the traditional lever-like moving keys with a soft rubber surface embedded with sensors, and some models have a built-in sound engine. The player controls pitch, timbre and dynamics through five kinds of sensing — strike, press, sideways slide, front-to-back slide and the speed of release — and can produce microtonal glides, vibrato and polyphonic aftertouch. It is used for playing electronic music, and with digital music software, or as a controller.

羅利海岸鍵盤為電鳴數位音樂介面（MIDI）鍵盤控制器，聲音由感測器輸出控制參數，: The Seaboard is an electrophone MIDI keyboard controller; its sound is generated by a sound engine from control parameters output by the sensors, not by hammers or by vibrating air. Its flexible, continuous key surface changes the sound according to how fast a key is struck, the pressure after the strike and sideways and front-to-back sliding, producing microtonal bends, glides, vibrato and changes of timbre; in a sound-source program, how hard a key is pressed controls volume, and the front-to-back slide mostly changes the filter cutoff frequency. The range depends on how many keys the model has, and the source does not list an actual pitch range. Compared with traditional MIDI keyboards, some models need no extra knobs or pitch wheel: the fingers on the key surface control pitch, timbre and sustain at once, closer to the continuous slide of a fretless string instrument or a wind instrument than to sounding only from discrete key positions.
